content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no pill that reliably stops a hangover, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. What you can buy falls into a few groups that do very different jobs. Painkiller pills like Blowfish and Alka-Seltzer genuinely ease a headache the morning after, but they come with stomach risks when alcohol is involved. DHM supplements, taken while you drink, have the most interesting research behind them, though most of it is from animals and the human evidence is still small. Probiotic "pre-drink" pills like Myrkl rest on a clever idea with very little human data on how people actually feel the next day. If you want to try a hangover pill, pick the group that matches what you're hoping for, keep your expectations modest, and treat it as an add-on to water, food, and pacing rather than a replacement for them.

**Our quick picks:** For a DHM supplement with the most "extras" in the formula, [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is our top choice. For the best balance of dose and price, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is hard to beat. If cost per dose is all you care about, [NusaPure DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08B32XBRB?tag=dhmguide-20) has the lowest price per 1,000 mg serving we track. For a morning-after headache, an aspirin-and-caffeine product such as Blowfish does help, as long as aspirin is safe for you. Details, trade-offs, and who should skip each one are below.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide compares products based on their labels and published research. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Most hangover pills are sold as dietary supplements, which the FDA does not review for safety or effectiveness before they go on sale. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before trying any hangover product if** you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver, kidney, stomach, or bleeding problems, or take any regular medicine, especially blood thinners, antidepressants, sedatives, seizure medicines, or diabetes medicine. **Get emergency help right away (call 911 in the US)** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, or has pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no pill helps with that.

## What "Hangover Pills" Actually Are

The phrase "hangover pills" covers products that work in completely different ways. Lumping them together is how people end up disappointed, so it helps to sort them first.

1. **Painkiller pills (taken the morning after).** These contain a real over-the-counter drug, usually aspirin, often with caffeine. Blowfish and Alka-Seltzer are the best-known examples. They treat symptoms, mainly headache and grogginess. They do nothing for the underlying causes of a hangover.
2. **DHM supplements (taken while drinking or before bed).** DHM, short for dihydromyricetin, is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis). Brands include No Days Wasted, Double Wood, Cheers, Flyby, Toniiq, and NusaPure. The idea is to support how your body handles alcohol, so you feel less rough the next day.
3. **Probiotic "pre-drink" pills (taken before drinking).** Myrkl is the main example. It contains bacteria chosen because they can break down alcohol, with the aim of reducing how much reaches your bloodstream.
4. **Vitamin, electrolyte, and herbal blends.** B vitamins, electrolytes, milk thistle, prickly pear, ginger, L-cysteine, and so on, either on their own or mixed into the products above.
5. **Activated charcoal.** Sold as a way to "absorb" alcohol. It doesn't do this well, and we don't recommend it (more on that below).

If you want the full evidence breakdown for each type, our article on [whether hangover pills actually work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-pills-actually-work) goes deeper into the research. This page is the buyer's guide: which products are worth your money and which ones to skip.

## Do Hangover Pills Work? What the Research Says

It's worth being blunt about the evidence before you spend anything.

A hangover isn't one problem. It's several at once: poor sleep, inflammation, stomach irritation, mild dehydration, the toxic by-product acetaldehyde that your liver makes while breaking down alcohol, and a rebound in brain chemistry as alcohol wears off. A pill that targets one of these can only ever help with part of the picture.

Two large reviews have looked at the research as a whole:

- **A 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ*** (Pittler, Verster, and Ernst) found no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary remedy prevented or treated hangovers.
- **A 2022 systematic review in *Addiction*** (from researchers at King's College London) found that a few ingredients, including Hovenia dulcis fruit extract, L-cysteine, clove extract, red ginseng, and Korean pear juice, showed some benefit in individual small studies. But the authors rated the quality of that evidence as very low and concluded that no remedy could be recommended with confidence.

So the honest framing is this. The best hangover pill can take the edge off for some people. None of them reliably prevents a hangover, and none of them can undo the effect of drinking a lot. The only method that works every time is drinking less, which our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers alongside the habits with the best evidence.

## How We Chose the Best Hangover Pills

We didn't run lab tests or a clinical trial. Here's what we looked at instead, and you can use the same checklist on any product you find:

- **What the active ingredient is, and how much.** For DHM products, the dose per serving matters. Products range from about 300 mg to 1,000 mg per serving, and there is no settled human dose, so we note it clearly for each one.
- **Cost per serving, not cost per bottle.** A cheap-looking box with four servings can cost more per night out than a bottle with 30.
- **Transparency.** We favor labels that list every ingredient and its amount over "proprietary blends" that hide the doses.
- **Sensible extras.** Some add-ins, like L-cysteine or milk thistle, have at least some research behind them. Others mostly pad the ingredient list.
- **Safety and fit.** Who should avoid the product, and whether it interacts with common medicines.

## How DHM Is Supposed to Work, and Where the Evidence Stands

DHM became popular after a 2012 study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* from a UCLA research group. In rats, DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal, apparently by acting on the brain's GABA receptors, the same system alcohol affects. Other lab and animal studies suggest DHM may help the body clear alcohol and acetaldehyde faster and may protect liver cells from alcohol-related stress.

Here's the honest catch: most of that research is in animals or cells. There are a few small human studies of Hovenia dulcis extracts (the plant DHM comes from), and they're among the ingredients the 2022 *Addiction* review flagged as worth more study. But there is no good evidence yet from large, independent human trials that DHM supplements prevent hangovers. Some people say they notice a clear difference. Others notice nothing.

That's why we describe DHM as promising rather than proven. If you want to try it, the usual approach is to take it while drinking or before bed, with water. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and you can compare every brand in our [supplement reviews](/reviews).

**Safety notes on DHM:** it's generally well tolerated in the studies done so far, but long-term human safety data are limited. Because it acts on GABA receptors, be cautious combining it with sedatives, sleep aids, or anti-anxiety medicines, and ask a pharmacist if you take any regular medicine. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains which combinations deserve a second look.

## Blowfish for Hangovers: Best for a Morning-After Headache

Blowfish is an effervescent tablet you dissolve in water. A dose of two tablets contains 1,000 mg of aspirin and caffeine. Unlike DHM supplements, it's an FDA-regulated over-the-counter drug, sold under the same rules as other aspirin-and-caffeine pain relievers.

- **What it does well:** aspirin eases a pounding head, and caffeine blunts the grogginess. For a headache-led hangover, it genuinely helps, and that isn't just placebo.
- **What it doesn't do:** it doesn't help much with nausea, doesn't rehydrate you beyond the glass of water you mix it in, and does nothing for the underlying causes.
- **The safety trade-off:** aspirin irritates the stomach lining and thins the blood, and alcohol irritates the stomach too. The US aspirin label warns about stomach bleeding for people who have three or more drinks a day.
- **Value:** you can get similar ingredients from generic aspirin plus a cup of coffee for less.

Take it the morning after, with food and water, not before bed while alcohol is still in your system. Skip it if you have ulcers, reflux, or bleeding problems, take blood thinners, are allergic to aspirin, are pregnant, or are under 18. Our full [Blowfish review](/never-hungover/blowfish-hangover-review) and our guide to [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) explain the risks in more detail.

## Alka-Seltzer for Hangovers: An Old Standby With a Salt Catch

Alka-Seltzer Original is another fizzy aspirin tablet. Each tablet contains 325 mg of aspirin with sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) and citric acid, which together act as an antacid. That makes it a reasonable fit for the classic "headache plus sour stomach" morning.

- **Pros:** cheap and easy to find; the antacid part can settle an upset stomach; the fizzy drink gets some water into you.
- **Cons:** it's still aspirin, with the same stomach-bleeding and blood-thinning concerns as Blowfish. It's also high in sodium, which matters if you have high blood pressure, heart or kidney problems, or have been told to limit salt.
- **Watch the name:** the Alka-Seltzer range includes many different products. Some "Plus" cold and flu versions contain different drugs, including acetaminophen (Tylenol) in some formulas. Always read the Drug Facts label so you know what you're taking, and don't double up on painkillers.

If acid and burning are your main symptoms rather than headache, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) covers gentler options. And if you're wondering whether a different painkiller would be better, our articles on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) compare the stomach and liver risks of each. In short: never take acetaminophen to "head off" a hangover, because alcohol and acetaminophen together can stress the liver.

## Myrkl: The Probiotic "Pre-Drink" Pill

Myrkl, from the Swedish company De Faire Medical, takes a different approach. You take it before drinking, and its probiotic bacteria are meant to start breaking down alcohol in your gut so less of it reaches your bloodstream.

- **Pros:** an interesting idea; more published human research than many hangover products; looks low risk for most healthy adults.
- **Cons:** the main human study was small, company-funded, and measured blood alcohol levels rather than how people felt the next morning. The theory also has a built-in limit, because alcohol is absorbed quickly and mostly processed in the liver, where gut bacteria can't reach.
- **Important:** Myrkl does not make you sober and must never be used to decide whether you're fine to drive.

There is no good evidence yet that Myrkl makes hangovers noticeably better for most people. Reviews online are split between people who swear by it and people who noticed nothing. Our full [Myrkl review](/never-hungover/myrkl-review) has the details. If you're interested in the probiotic idea, [ZBiotics](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) is a related product, though it's a drink rather than a pill and targets acetaldehyde instead of alcohol itself.

## Other Ingredients You'll See in Hangover Pills

Most hangover supplements mix several of the ingredients below. Here's a quick, honest read on each:

- **Prickly pear (Opuntia).** A small randomized trial published in 2004 in *Archives of Internal Medicine* found prickly pear extract reduced some hangover symptoms, such as nausea and dry mouth, but not all of them. Our [DHM vs prickly pear comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-prickly-pear-hangovers) looks at both.
- **L-cysteine.** An amino acid that helps the body make glutathione, an antioxidant involved in clearing acetaldehyde. A small Finnish study suggested some benefit. Our [L-cysteine guide](/never-hungover/l-cysteine-for-hangover) covers the details.
- **Milk thistle.** The best-known liver herb. Human results for liver health are mixed, and there's little direct hangover research.
- **B vitamins and electrolytes.** Alcohol can affect how you absorb and use some nutrients, and B vitamins and electrolytes are common add-ins. They're low risk, but there's little evidence that they prevent hangovers on their own.
- **Hovenia and turmeric products from Korea and Japan.** These are hugely popular in East Asia. See our guide to [Korean and Japanese hangover pills](/never-hungover/korean-japanese-hangover-pills) for what's in them.
- **Activated charcoal.** We'd skip it. Charcoal binds alcohol poorly, and it can interfere with the absorption of medicines you take around the same time. Our [activated charcoal article](/never-hungover/activated-charcoal-hangover) explains why.

## Hangover Pills to Be Careful With

Some products deserve extra caution, either because of what's in them or how they're used.

- **"Night-time" or "PM" products.** Anything containing a sedating antihistamine (like diphenhydramine or doxylamine) adds drowsiness on top of alcohol. Don't combine them the same night you drink.
- **Anything with acetaminophen.** Check labels for acetaminophen, APAP, or paracetamol, especially in multi-symptom "morning after" products. Never take it before bed after drinking.
- **Products with hidden doses.** "Proprietary blends" list ingredients but not amounts, so you can't tell whether you're getting a meaningful dose of anything.
- **Big promises.** Be wary of any label that says it will stop a hangover completely or let you drink more without consequences. No product has good evidence for that.
- **Stacking several products.** Taking a DHM supplement, a painkiller pill, and a night-time sleep aid together multiplies the chance of side effects and interactions.

## How to Use Hangover Pills Sensibly

If you decide to try one, a few habits make a bigger difference than which brand you pick:

1. **Match the pill to the job.** DHM and probiotic products are taken before or while drinking. Painkiller pills are for the morning after, never before bed.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption.
3. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between drinks is simple and helps. If you want more, our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade comparison](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) covers rehydration drinks.
4. **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies from person to person. No pill speeds that up enough to matter for driving.
5. **Protect your sleep.** Much of next-day fog is simply poor sleep.
6. **Try one product at a time.** If you change three things at once, you won't know what helped.

For a full checklist of what to do before a night out, our guide on [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking) pulls it together, and our [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas) cover what to keep on hand.

## When a Hangover Means You Should See a Doctor

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless and pass within a day. Some symptoms are a sign of something more serious. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US)** if someone who has been drinking:

- is confused, can't stay awake, or can't be woken
- is vomiting while drowsy or vomiting repeatedly
- has slow, shallow, or irregular breathing
- has pale or bluish skin or feels very cold
- has a seizure

Also see a doctor if you notice black or tarry stools or vomit that looks like coffee grounds after taking aspirin, if you have severe stomach pain, or if you might have taken more acetaminophen than the label allows (call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** in the US, even if you feel fine).

If you get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or have a racing heart when you go a day or two without drinking, that's different from a hangover. It can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous, so talk to a doctor rather than trying to manage it with supplements.

## The Bottom Line

- No hangover pill reliably prevents a hangover. The best ones can take the edge off for some people.
- **For a DHM supplement:** [No Days Wasted](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) if you want the most complete formula, [Double Wood](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) for the best balance of dose and price, or [NusaPure](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08B32XBRB?tag=dhmguide-20) for the lowest cost per dose.
- **For a morning-after headache:** an aspirin-and-caffeine product like Blowfish helps, or Alka-Seltzer if your stomach is sour too, as long as aspirin is safe for you. Take it with food, never before bed.
- **For Myrkl and other probiotics:** an interesting idea, but expect little.
- Water, food, pacing, and sleep still matter more than any pill.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best hangover pill?**

It depends on what you want it to do. For a supplement taken while drinking, a DHM product is the most popular choice, with No Days Wasted offering the most complete formula and Double Wood the best value. For a morning-after headache, an aspirin-and-caffeine product like Blowfish works for many people. No pill reliably prevents a hangover, so treat any of them as an add-on to water, food, and pacing.

**Do hangover pills actually work?**

Some can help a little, but none are reliable. Large research reviews have found no strong evidence that any pill prevents or cures a hangover. Painkiller pills can ease a headache. DHM has promising animal research and limited human data. A few ingredients, such as prickly pear and L-cysteine, have small studies suggesting modest benefits for some symptoms.

**When should I take a hangover pill?**

It depends on the type. DHM supplements and probiotic products like Myrkl are taken before or while drinking, or before bed. Painkiller pills like Blowfish and Alka-Seltzer are for the morning after, taken with food and water. Never take aspirin, ibuprofen, or acetaminophen before bed while alcohol is still in your system.

**Is Alka-Seltzer good for a hangover?**

Alka-Seltzer Original combines aspirin with an antacid, so it can help with a headache and an upset stomach at the same time. But it's still aspirin, which can irritate a stomach already irritated by alcohol, and it's high in sodium. Check the label, since some Alka-Seltzer Plus cold products contain other drugs, including acetaminophen in some formulas.

**Is Blowfish better than DHM?**

They do different jobs. Blowfish is an aspirin-and-caffeine pain reliever for the morning after, and it genuinely eases headaches for many people, but it doesn't address anything beyond symptoms and carries stomach risks with alcohol. DHM is taken while drinking and aims to support how your body handles alcohol, but the human evidence is still limited. Some people use DHM while drinking and save a painkiller for the morning only if they need it.

**Does Myrkl work?**

There is no good evidence yet that Myrkl makes hangovers noticeably better for most people. Its main human study was small, company-funded, and measured blood alcohol rather than how people felt the next day. It looks low risk for healthy adults, but it does not make you sober and should never be used to judge whether you're fine to drive.

**Are hangover pills safe?**

Most are low risk for healthy adults when used as directed, but "supplement" doesn't mean risk-free. Aspirin-based pills can cause stomach bleeding when combined with alcohol. DHM may interact with sedatives and some other medicines. Products sold as supplements aren't reviewed by the FDA before sale. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist first if you take regular medicine, are pregnant, or have liver, kidney, stomach, or bleeding problems.

**Can I take a hangover pill and still drive?**

No. No hangover pill lowers your blood alcohol fast enough to make driving safe, and none of them make you sober. Your body clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour, and that varies a lot between people. If you've been drinking, don't drive.
